books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, D. The Women's Rights Movement

primary_sources: Sarah Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, 1838

stimulus.text: "But I ask no favors for my sex. I surrender not our claim to equality. All I ask of our brethren is, that they will take their feet from off our necks, and permit us to stand upright on that ground which God designed us to occupy." — Sarah Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, 1838
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Sarah Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes (Boston: Isaac Knapp, 1838), Letter II, written July 1837. Wording checked against the Project Gutenberg edition. Note: the passage is Sarah Grimké's, not her sister Angelina's.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Sarah Grimké, Letters (1838)
stem: Why would Grimké's letter have struck readers in 1838 as especially powerful?

options.text: She was a formerly enslaved person writing about slavery herself
options.misconception: Grimké was white, the daughter of a slaveholder; she was never enslaved.

options.text: She was a Catholic nun writing about the church's teachings
options.misconception: Grimké was a Quaker convert, not a nun, and the letter is about equality, not the church.

options.text: She was a Massachusetts legislator writing a new law
options.misconception: Women could not serve in legislatures in 1838; Grimké wrote letters, not laws.

options.text: She was raised in a slaveholding family and knew slavery firsthand

rationales.A: Sarah Grimké was born white into a wealthy Charleston slaveholding family. She witnessed slavery as an owner, not as an enslaved person.
rationales.B: The Grimkés converted to Quakerism, not Catholicism. The letter claims equality, not church reform.
rationales.C: No woman served in a state legislature in 1838. Grimké's power came from her pen and her witness, not from office.
rationales.D: Grimké grew up in a slaveholder's house in Charleston and saw slavery's cruelties daily. Her testimony carried the weight of an insider.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who writes. A daughter of a Charleston slaveholder, writing against slavery and for women.
2. Ask what she saw. She grew up watching slavery's cruelties in her own home.
3. Name the power. An insider who breaks with her own class is hard to dismiss.
Background: Angelina Grimké, Sarah's younger sister, became the more famous speaker; Sarah became the more systematic writer.
Remember: a witness from inside the system hits harder than one from outside — ask where the writer stood.
